_note: Ranking the World's Easiest Languages (for English speakers). Rank = FSI weeks of class (U.S. Foreign Service Institute), ties broken by the share of the 207 Swadesh core words that look like English (easy_score.py, Wiktionary Swadesh appendices). Each example word is a real Lingua Libre recording of a word that looks like its English twin.
title: Ranking the World's Easiest Languages
subtitle: FOR ENGLISH SPEAKERS, BY CLASS TIME NEEDED
meter: Weeks of class to learn it (FSI)
outro: Which language was easiest for you?

items.name: Dutch
cards: The U.S. diplomats' school (FSI) says about 24 weeks (600 class hours) of full-time study. And 37% of the 207 core words look like their English twins.
Dutch is English's closest big relative: 'appel' is apple, 'water' is water, 'hand' is hand. The catch: verbs jump to the end of some sentences.

items.name: Norwegian
cards: The U.S. diplomats' school (FSI) says about 24 weeks (600 class hours) of full-time study. And 36% of the 207 core words look like their English twins.
Norwegian verbs never change for the person: jeg er, du er, han er means I am, you are, he is. No cases, no conjugation tables.

items.name: Swedish
cards: The U.S. diplomats' school (FSI) says about 24 weeks (600 class hours) of full-time study. And 35% of the 207 core words look like their English twins.
Swedish verbs don't change for the person either (jag är, du är). The hard part is the sing-song melody: some words differ only by their pitch.

items.name: Danish
cards: The U.S. diplomats' school (FSI) says about 24 weeks (600 class hours) of full-time study. And 34% of the 207 core words look like their English twins.
Danish grammar is easy, the sounds are not: Danes swallow so many consonants that even Swedes and Norwegians struggle to understand them.

items.name: Italian
cards: The U.S. diplomats' school (FSI) says about 24 weeks (600 class hours) of full-time study. And 22% of the 207 core words look like their English twins.
Italian is written almost exactly as it sounds, and thousands of English words share its Latin roots: famiglia, family; notte, nocturnal.

items.name: Spanish
cards: The U.S. diplomats' school (FSI) says about 24 weeks (600 class hours) of full-time study. And 20% of the 207 core words look like their English twins.
English got 'chocolate' from Spanish, which took it from Nahuatl, the Aztec language. Spanish is spelled the way it sounds, with only five vowel sounds.

items.name: Romanian
cards: The U.S. diplomats' school (FSI) says about 24 weeks (600 class hours) of full-time study. And 20% of the 207 core words look like their English twins.
Romanian is the Latin language of Eastern Europe: lună is the moon, as in 'lunar'. The twist: 'the' goes at the end, lup is wolf, lupul is the wolf.

items.name: Portuguese
cards: The U.S. diplomats' school (FSI) says about 24 weeks (600 class hours) of full-time study. And 19% of the 207 core words look like their English twins.
Many Portuguese words are spelled like English (animal, hotel, hospital), but the nasal vowels, like in pão (bread), take practice.

items.name: French
cards: The U.S. diplomats' school (FSI) says about 30 weeks (750 class hours) of full-time study. And 21% of the 207 core words look like their English twins.
Around 30% of English words come from French, after the Norman conquest of 1066. But French needs 30 weeks: silent letters and tricky sounds.

items.name: German
cards: The U.S. diplomats' school (FSI) says about 36 weeks (900 class hours) of full-time study. And 36% of the 207 core words look like their English twins.
German core words look most like English (Hand, Haus, Wasser), but it needs 36 weeks: three genders and four cases give 'the' six forms.
